message:
SITUATION:
Our assembly line can only start a production run when parts from all three of our suppliers have arrived. Each supplier independently delivers on time 90% of the time. Our operations director said in the review, with total confidence: "Every supplier is 90% reliable, so we start on time 90% of the time. That's the number we'll quote to the customer." It sounds right to me; they're all at 90%, so the whole chain is at 90%. Can we quote 90% on-time starts to the customer?

CLAIM:
If each of three independent suppliers is on time 90% of the time and all three are needed, runs start on time 90% of the time.

RESPONSE:
**No. Quoting 90% would overpromise.** If the three suppliers really are independent, you start on time only about **73%** of the time.

### Why

A run needs **all three** deliveries on time. With independent suppliers, you multiply the probabilities:

0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = **0.729**, or about 73%

| Outcome | Probability |
|---|---|
| All three on time (start on time) | 72.9% |
| Exactly one late | 24.3% |
| Exactly two late | 2.7% |
| All three late | 0.1% |

Roughly **1 run in 4** would start late, not 1 in 10. Each supplier is a separate chance for something to go wrong, and the chances add up. The more suppliers you need at once, the lower the joint rate. With five suppliers at 90%, it would be about 59%.

The director's reasoning would only hold if the suppliers always failed together (all late or all on time). That's the opposite of independence.

### What we don't know

The 73% figure depends on two assumptions:

1. **Independence.** You said they deliver independently, but shared causes can link them: weather, port congestion, a shared carrier, or holiday peaks. Linked lateness pushes the real rate somewhere between 73% and 90%. Independence is the cautious case.
2. **What "on time" means.** If a supplier's "on time" includes a grace window, or you hold buffer stock that absorbs small delays, your effective rate could be higher.

**What would settle it:** your own production records. Count the runs over the past period that actually started on time, or check delivery logs for how often all three arrived together. That observed rate is the number to quote, ideally with a little margin.

### Options if 73% isn't good enough to quote

- **Safety stock** of each supplier's parts, so one late delivery doesn't stop the line
- **Dual-sourcing** the least reliable part
- **Earlier order or delivery windows** so late deliveries still land before the start
- **Quoting a longer lead time** that builds in slack

My suggestion: don't quote 90% based on this reasoning. Quote about 73%, or your measured historical rate, until mitigations or real data justify a higher number.
